p.x:
Last Saturday, our school organised a beach clean-up in Rayong. About fifty students and teachers took part. We arrived at 8 a.m., and each of us got gloves and a big bag. The beach looked beautiful from far away, but when we walked on the sand, we found a lot of rubbish. There were plastic bottles, straws, food boxes and even an old shoe!
In three hours, we collected more than 200 kilograms of rubbish. Our teacher explained that much of it comes from the sea, not from people on the beach. "Plastic in the water can kill turtles and fish," she said. After lunch, we sorted the rubbish. We put bottles and cans in a special bin so they could be recycled.
I felt tired but happy. The beach was clean again, and we learned that we need to protect nature. Now my family tries not to waste plastic. We take our own bags when we go shopping, and we save water at home.

Many people think that only governments and big companies can stop global warming. But our daily choices also matter. Here are some easy changes anyone can make.
Start in the kitchen. Choose fruit and vegetables with less packaging, and bring reusable containers to the market. If possible, buy organic food from local farmers; it travels a shorter distance and often uses fewer harmful chemicals. Never drop litter: plastic wrappers on the street end up in rivers and the sea, where they damage wildlife.
At home, switch off electricity you aren't using, and consider solar panels if you own your house. On the road, every litre of fuel you burn adds carbon to the air. Walking, cycling or sharing a car can make a real difference. Finally, before you throw something away, ask yourself: can I reuse or repair it? Most things can have a second life.

For decades, recycling has been presented as the answer to our waste problem. Yet only around 9% of all plastic ever produced has actually been recycled. The rest has been burned, dumped in landfill sites, or left to contaminate rivers and oceans, where it breaks down into tiny particles that enter the food chain. Some plastics also release toxic chemicals as they degrade.
Environmental experts now argue that we need to rethink the entire system. The first step is to produce less. Companies are being encouraged to design products that are reusable, repairable or truly biodegradable, and to replace oil-based plastics with materials made from renewable sources such as plants. At home, food scraps that would otherwise rot in landfill and release methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, can be turned into compost.
Such changes are part of a wider move towards a sustainable economy, one that does not rely on the depletion of natural resources. Individuals can help reduce their own carbon footprint, but experts stress that consumer action alone cannot mitigate the problem. Without stronger laws and investment, the plastic tide will keep rising.
